content: SUNY Downstate Medical Center, officially known as the State University of New York Health Science Center at Brooklyn, is an academic medical center and the only institution of its kind in Brooklyn, New York City. In 1858, the Long Island College Hospital was granted permission by the state to establish a medical school, making it the first hospital-based medical school in the United States. In 1931, the institution was rechartered as the Long Island College of Medicine. On April 5, 1950, the school became known as Downstate following a merger between the Long Island College of Medicine and the newly formed State University of New York. SUNY Downstate Medical Center comprises a College of Medicine, a College of Health Related Professions, a College of Nursing, a School of Graduate Studies, and the University Hospital of Brooklyn. The institution currently enrolls 1,516 students, with 50% of them being minorities or recent immigrants. The College of Medicine at SUNY Downstate has the highest percentage of minority students among all medical schools in New York State. The current president of the institution is Dr. John C. LaRosa. Educational Achievements SUNY Downstate Medical Center was the first hospital-based medical school in the United States. It also established the first hospital-based nurse-midwifery training program in the country and the first bachelor's degree program in medical sonography. Nationally, it ranks eighth in the number of alumni who serve as faculty members at American medical schools. Among the nearly 21,000 physicians practicing in New York City, more graduated from SUNY Downstate than from any other medical school. Regional Economic Impact SUNY Downstate Medical Center is the fifth-largest employer in Brooklyn. Approximately 85% of its employees reside in New York City, with 62% living in Brooklyn. The institution's total economic impact on New York State, including direct, indirect, and induced effects, exceeds $627 million. For every $1 invested by the state, SUNY Downstate generates more than $12 in economic returns. The lifetime earning potential for graduates in nursing and allied health fields increases by $288,000 to $925,000. In the 1998-1999 fiscal year, the institution secured $47 million in external research funding, including $24 million from federal sources. Notable Contributions to Medicine and Research SUNY Downstate was home to the inventor of the heart-lung machine, who performed the first successful open-heart surgery in New York State. The institution established the nation's first federally funded dialysis program at the University Hospital of Brooklyn. Researchers at SUNY Downstate produced the first human images using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A distinguished professor of psychiatry and neuroscience published a landmark study demonstrating that children of alcoholics may have a higher risk of developing alcoholism. In 1986, SUNY Downstate conducted the first federally funded study on the transmission of HIV from mother to fetus. In 1998, Dr. Robert Furchgott, a distinguished professor emeritus of pharmacology, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine for his groundbreaking research on nitric oxide. In 2006, Drs. Todd Sacktor and Andre Fenton conducted research on the maintenance of long-term potentiation and its implications for spatial memory storage. This work was recognized as one of the top scientific breakthroughs of the year by Science magazine. References in Popular Culture In his 1999 song Got, Mos Def references SUNY Downstate Medical Center with the line, you takin' a ride on the Downstate Medical, implying that a victim of a violent robbery might be transported by ambulance to SUNY Downstate for medical care.
